title: WeaveVLA Lifts LIBERO-Plus Success from 74.9% to 82.0%
summary: HKUST and PolyU release WeaveVLA on November 24, 2026, a framework that enhances vision-language-action models with 3D relational reasoning for robotics.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- HKUST and PolyU researchers released WeaveVLA on November 24, 2026, adding task-conditioned 3D relation graphs to vision-language-action models.
- WeaveVLA pushes StarVLA-GR00T success on LIBERO-Plus from 74.9% to 82.0% and π0.5 from 85.7% to 87.8%, both clearing 98% on LIBERO.
- Real-world physical task success climbs from 55.6% to 70.0% under standard conditions and 33.3% to 53.3% under distribution shifts.


Researchers from the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and Hong Kong Polytechnic University released WeaveVLA on November 24, 2026, a framework that enhances vision-language-action models with explicit 3D relational reasoning. The system pushes StarVLA-GR00T from 74.9% to 82.0% success on the LIBERO-Plus benchmark and lifts π0.5 from 85.7% to 87.8%, with both configurations clearing 98% average success on the standard LIBERO suite. Real-world physical task performance climbs from 55.6% to 70.0% under standard conditions and from 33.3% to 53.3% under out-of-distribution perturbations.


## Release Date and Availability


The WeaveVLA framework was officially released on November 24, 2026, with a preprint posted November 23, 2026. The research comes from a collaboration between HKUST and PolyU robotics labs and is available through standard academic channels. The framework builds on two existing vision-language-action backbones: StarVLA-GR00T and π0.5, adding a task-conditioned graph neural network layer that models pairwise 3D relations among objects, the robot gripper, and task references.


## Architecture and Technical Approach


WeaveVLA adds a sparse graph neural network that explicitly tracks geometric relationships between objects in a robotic manipulation scene. The system maintains pair-specific recurrent edge states that integrate geometric evidence across observation frames, allowing the model to reason about how spatial relationships evolve during task execution. A learned-query readout mechanism summarizes the updated graph representations into compact relational tokens, which condition the action expert alongside the original vision-language context from the base model.


The framework includes an auxiliary geometry reconstruction objective that preserves spatial structure during training. This design choice ensures that the graph representations remain grounded in physical 3D space rather than drifting into abstract feature spaces. The task-conditioned nature of the graph allows the system to focus on task-relevant relations while ignoring irrelevant object pairs, reducing computational overhead.


## Benchmark Performance and Real-World Results


On the LIBERO-Plus benchmark, WeaveVLA demonstrates clear gains across both tested backbones. The StarVLA-GR00T configuration improves from 74.9% to 82.0% success rate, while the π0.5 backbone advances from 85.7% to 87.8%. Both configurations achieve over 98% average success on the standard LIBERO suite, though these figures approach saturation on that benchmark.


Real-world physical experiments provide more informative performance bounds. Testing on three physical manipulation tasks, the StarVLA-GR00T variant climbs from 55.6% to 70.0% under standard conditions. When subjected to out-of-distribution perturbations, including object position shifts and appearance changes, success rates improve from 33.3% to 53.3%. These gains suggest that explicit 3D relational reasoning helps models generalize beyond training distribution constraints.


## Research Context and Timing


The WeaveVLA release arrives on the same day as ReWeave, another LIBERO-family result logged by robotics research feeds. This timing reflects ongoing parallel work in the vision-language-action space, where multiple research groups are exploring different approaches to grounding language-conditioned policies in spatial reasoning. The framework demonstrates that augmenting pre-trained vision-language-action models with structured geometric representations can yield consistent gains without full retraining.


## What This Means


WeaveVLA validates the hypothesis that explicit 3D relation modeling can improve vision-language-action models for robotic manipulation. The consistent gains across two different base models and multiple benchmarks suggest the approach is robust and generalizable. The real-world performance improvements, particularly under distribution shifts, indicate that structured geometric reasoning helps models handle the variability present in physical environments. For robotics researchers, the framework offers a concrete path to augmenting existing vision-language-action architectures with spatial reasoning capabilities without requiring complete model redesigns.
